VIS104 · WEEK 04 · ANALOG DRAWING

Conditions, Shared State, and Emergence

A group can produce a coherent drawing by responding to the same changing page. Roles, local conditions and turn-taking organize a result that no participant plans in advance.

How can a group make one coherent work without a master image?

Reference works

01 / LECTURE

Lecture overview

  • Input and mappingMorellet shows how an external sequence can activate a fixed visual rule.
  • Roles and shared stateEach participant reads the current drawing before choosing an action.
  • Conditions and recoveryLegal moves, tied choices, blocked turns and stopping rules make the system executable.
  • EmergenceLocal responses and repeated updates create global organization over time.

02 / LAB · EXECUTE A CLASSIC WORK

Execute Hatching and The Beach

Groups of four execute two Conditional Design works. The pair contrasts interacting geometric conditions with a repeated perceptual judgment.

  1. Set the roles. Keep one black, blue, red or green pen per participant and a consistent clockwise order.
  2. Hatching. Connect existing dots at the angle allowed for the active color. Seek a short legal connection, hatch eligible enclosures and add a new dot beyond the current hull.
  3. The Beach. Read the entire dot field, judge where the largest empty region lies, and place one dot near its perceived center.
  4. Compare the systems. Observe how the next action depends on the current page in each case. Document the resulting group drawings.

The class follows the published works with classroom clarifications for angle boundaries, tied choices, blocked moves and stopping. These clarifications belong to the course adaptation.

StudyProcedureWhat becomes visible
HatchingAngle, connection, enclosure and expansion conditions.A growing network with hatched planes.
The BeachOne repeated judgment about empty space.An increasingly distributed field of dots.

03 / EXERCISE · DESIGN AN ORIGINAL WORK

Design a Conditional Drawing

Each student designs an original drawing activity for 3–4 other participants. Their marks must respond to a shared state and change what becomes possible next.

  1. Design the relations. Specify roles, a starting state, turn order and a mark vocabulary. Build at least one dependency on another mark, role or visible spatial condition.
  2. Make the system runnable. State an observable if/when condition, meaningful participant choices, conflict handling and a stopping rule.
  3. Observe a test. Give the written score to the group and observe without directing the drawing. Record a pause, ambiguity, deadlock or unexpected relation.
  4. Revise and rerun. Change the relevant rule and execute the revised score on a fresh A2 sheet. Document early, middle and final states.

Execution reveals what a condition does; the exercise asks students to invent and test a new relationship.

References for student design

These works offer ways to structure a new system. Students develop their own instruction and relationships.

Outputs

Lab
Two collective drawings, one for each published system, with photographs.
Exercise
An original group score in editable Word and print, one A2 realization, early/middle/final images and an 80–120-word revision note.
